methods.title: High-Definition Sewer Camera Lateral Scope
methods.whenItFits: The most critical component of a thorough plumbing inspection, visually verifying underground sewer health out to the street main.
methods.text: We feed a self-leveling color optical camera with radio sonde through cleanouts, recording video footage of pipe walls, joints, and slope.

methods.title: Water Pressure & Static Leak Decay Testing
methods.whenItFits: Essential for testing incoming municipal water pressure and proving whether hidden pinhole pipe leaks exist.
methods.text: We attach calibrated test gauges to measure static street PSI, check pressure-reducing valve operation, and monitor low-flow meter dials.

methods.title: Comprehensive 50-Point Visual Fixture & Tank Audit
methods.whenItFits: Complete hands-on inspection of every visible plumbing fixture, shutoff valve, water heater, and drain in the home.
methods.text: We test water heater anode rods and relief valves, inspect supply lines under sinks, test toilet flappers, and verify emergency shutoffs.

phoenixAngle.heading: Why Desert Soil & Aggressive Water Demand Specialized Phoenix Inspections
paragraphs: Plumbing inspections in the Phoenix Valley require specialized regional expertise. General home inspectors typically turn on faucets and flush toilets, but standard inspections fail to assess the harsh underground realities of the Sonoran Desert. Beneath our homes lie expansive clay and caliche soils that shift during monsoons, causing unseen breaks in buried cast-iron or clay sewer laterals.

Furthermore, Phoenix's intense mineral hardness causes severe internal calcification inside water heaters and behind shower mixing valves long before leaks become visible on finished drywall. Our certified master plumbers know exactly where Phoenix homes fail—from corroded polybutylene supply lines in 1980s subdivisions to failing orangeburg and clay laterals in historic Central Phoenix—giving you actionable peace of mind.

facts.text: Hidden sewer lateral collapses and calcified under-slab leaks represent the most common undetected plumbing defects in Phoenix homes.

faqs.q: What is included in a whole-home plumbing inspection in Phoenix?
faqs.a: A thorough plumbing inspection includes testing municipal water pressure, testing the pressure-reducing valve (PRV), inspecting the water heater and expansion tank, checking all under-sink shutoff valves and supply lines, testing toilets and faucets, and performing a full sewer camera lateral inspection.

faqs.q: Why should I get a plumbing inspection if I already had a home inspection?
faqs.a: General home inspectors only test visible fixture operation; they do not possess specialized optical cameras to inspect underground sewer pipes, nor do they perform static pressure decay tests. A dedicated plumbing inspection uncovers hidden sewer collapses, tree roots, and concealed under-slab leaks.

faqs.q: How long does a whole-home plumbing inspection take?
faqs.a: Most residential plumbing inspections take between 60 to 90 minutes to complete. Our licensed plumber thoroughly examines every fixture, runs video camera scopes through exterior cleanouts, tests water pressures, and reviews all video footage and prioritized repair recommendations with you in person.

faqs.q: What is polybutylene pipe, and why is it dangerous in Phoenix homes?
faqs.a: Polybutylene is a flexible gray plastic pipe widely installed in Phoenix homes between 1978 and 1995. Chlorine disinfectants in municipal water cause the plastic to flake and become brittle from the inside out, leading to catastrophic sudden pipe splits that flood homes without warning.

faqs.q: Do I receive a copy of the sewer camera video footage?
faqs.a: Yes, absolutely. Following the inspection, we provide you with a full digital video recording of the entire sewer camera scope, along with timestamped photos and an official written technician evaluation that can be submitted to sellers or kept for your home records.

faqs.q: How much water pressure should my Phoenix home have?
faqs.a: Residential water pressure should ideally sit between 50 and 65 PSI. If street pressure exceeds 80 PSI, it violates uniform plumbing code and will damage water heater tanks, cause dripping faucets, and blow out toilet fill valves. A pressure-reducing valve is required.
